claim: Thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways connecting the medial prefrontal cortex and the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) contribute to adaptive decision-making.
source: We recently showed that thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways connecting the medial prefrontal cortex and the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) contribute to adaptive decision-making (Alcaraz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2018).

claim: Crossed MD and OFC lesions did not impair instrumental performance.
source: Crossed MD and OFC lesions did not impair instrumental performance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disconnecting the OFC from the submedius nucleus produced a specific impairment in adaptive responding following action-outcome reversal.
source: Using the same approach, we found however that disconnecting the OFC from its other main thalamic afferent, the submedius nucleus, produced a specific impairment in adaptive responding following action-outcome reversal.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Multiple thalamocortical circuits may act synergistically to achieve behaviorally relevant functions.
source: Altogether, this suggests that multiple thalamocortical circuits may act synergistically to achieve behaviorally relevant functions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Goal-directed behaviors rely on highly flexible cognitive processes that appear to be largely supported by prefrontal cortical areas.
source: A large literature has documented that such goal-directed behaviors rely on highly flexible cognitive processes that appear to be largely supported by prefrontal cortical areas (O'Doherty et al., 2017; Parkes and Coutureau, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (O'Doherty et al., 2017; Parkes and Coutureau, 2018).

claim: Functional interactions between prefrontal and subcortical areas are essential to support goal-directed behaviors.
source: However, mounting experimental evidence indicates that functional interactions between prefrontal and subcortical areas are essential to support these functions (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Verschure et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Verschure et al., 2014).

claim: The contribution of several thalamic nuclei is now better understood and acknowledged in current views on the functioning of thalamocortical circuits.
source: In particular, the contribution of several thalamic nuclei is now better understood and acknowledged in current views on the functioning of thalamocortical circuits (Pergola et al., 2018; Rikhye et al., 2018b; Wolff and Vann, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent literature (Pergola et al., 2018; Rikhye et al., 2018b; Wolff and Vann, 2019).

claim: The interactions between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) have been highlighted in multiple behavioral setups and through various causal interventions.
source: Recently, the interactions between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) have been highlighted in multiple behavioral setups and through various causal interventions (Bradfield et al., 2013; Browning et al., 2015; Bolkan et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2017; Alcaraz et al., 2018; Marton et al., 2018; Rikhye et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways connecting the mPFC and the MD support complementary but dissociable aspects of goal-directed behavior.
source: For instance, we recently reported that thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways connecting the mPFC and the MD support complementary but dissociable aspects of goal-directed behavior (Alcaraz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2018).

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is one of the main cortical targets of MD projections.
source: However, the mPFC is not the only cortical recipient of MD projections as the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is also one of its main cortical targets (Groenewegen, 1988; Alcaraz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Groenewegen, 1988; Alcaraz et al., 2016).

claim: The OFC has long been associated with stimulus-outcome predictions.
source: Interestingly, while the OFC has long been associated with stimulus-outcome predictions (Balleine et al., 2011; McDannald et al., 2014; Stalnaker et al., 2014), its contribution to flexible goal-directed responding has now also been highlighted (Gremel and Costa, 2013; Bradfield et al., 2015; Bradfield et al., 2018; Panayi and Killcross, 2018; Parkes et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Balleine et al., 2011; McDannald et al., 2014; Stalnaker et al., 2014).

claim: The OFC's contribution to flexible goal-directed responding has been highlighted.
source: Interestingly, while the OFC has long been associated with stimulus-outcome predictions (Balleine et al., 2011; McDannald et al., 2014; Stalnaker et al., 2014), its contribution to flexible goal-directed responding has now also been highlighted (Gremel and Costa, 2013; Bradfield et al., 2015; Bradfield et al., 2018; Panayi and Killcross, 2018; Parkes et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent literature (Gremel and Costa, 2013; Bradfield et al., 2015; Bradfield et al., 2018; Panayi and Killcross, 2018; Parkes et al., 2018).

claim: The OFC is the recipient of a massive projection from the submedius thalamus (Sub).
source: Beyond MD afferents, the OFC is also the recipient of a massive projection from the submedius thalamus (Sub) (Yoshida et al., 1992; Alcaraz et al., 2015; Kuramoto et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Yoshida et al., 1992; Alcaraz et al., 2015; Kuramoto et al., 2017).

claim: The submedius thalamus was demonstrated to support the updating of stimulus-outcome associations, in a manner that was highly reminiscent of OFC functions.
source: While this region is currently poorly understood, it was recently demonstrated to support the updating of stimulus-outcome associations, in a manner that was highly reminiscent of OFC functions (Alcaraz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2015).

claim: A complex interplay occurs between the OFC and its thalamic afferents when flexible responding is essential.
source: This suggests that a complex interplay occurs between the OFC and its thalamic afferents when flexible responding is essential.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature on OFC and thalamic functions.

claim: The cortical lesions targeted mostly the lateral (LO) and the ventral (VO) parts of the orbitofrontal cortex.
source: In general, the lesions targeted mostly the lateral (LO) and the ventral (VO) parts of the orbitofrontal cortex and in most cases the medial orbital region (MO) was intact.
evidence: This describes the anatomical characteristics of the lesions performed in the study.

claim: In most cases the medial orbital region (MO) was intact after OFC lesions.
source: In general, the lesions targeted mostly the lateral (LO) and the ventral (VO) parts of the orbitofrontal cortex and in most cases the medial orbital region (MO) was intact.
evidence: This describes the anatomical characteristics of the lesions performed in the study.

claim: NMDA injections within the MD produced variable damage encompassing the three segments of the MD and, in many instances, the adjacent intralaminar nuclei.
source: NMDA injections within the MD produced variable damage (Figure 1B and E). Inclusions harbored significant damage encompassing the three segments of the MD and, in many instances, the adjacent intralaminar nuclei (mostly the paracentral and the centrolateral nuclei).
evidence: This describes the anatomical characteristics of the lesions performed in the study, with reference to Figure 1B and E.

claim: Sub lesions were largely in line with previous work and highly specific.
source: Sub lesions (Figure 1C and F) were largely in line with previous work (Alcaraz et al., 2015) and highly specific.
evidence: This describes the anatomical characteristics of the lesions performed in the study, with reference to Figure 1C and F and citation to prior work.

claim: Thalamic damage did not overlap between the MD and the Sub for any of the included rats.
source: Importantly, thalamic damage did not overlap between the MD and the Sub for any of the included rats.
evidence: This describes the specificity of the lesions performed in the study.

claim: Instrumental conditioning gradually developed over the 10 consecutive training sessions in Experiment 1.
source: Instrumental conditioning gradually developed over the 10 consecutive training sessions.
evidence: This describes the behavioral results from Experiment 1, supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Learning appeared to establish at similar rates in IPSI and CONTRA groups in Experiment 1.
source: As evident in Figure 3A, learning appeared to establish at similar rates in IPSI and CONTRA groups even though asymptotic performance appeared somewhat lower in the CONTRA group.
evidence: This describes the behavioral results from Experiment 1, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant effect of Session on instrumental conditioning in Experiment 1 (F(9,108) = 69.5, p<0.0001).
source: The statistical analysis supported these observations as the ANOVA revealed a significant effect of Session (F(9,108) = 69.5, p<0.0001) but the effect of Lesion only approached significance (F(1,12) = 3.5, p=0.0853).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The effect of Lesion on instrumental conditioning in Experiment 1 only approached significance (F(1,12) = 3.5, p=0.0853).
source: The statistical analysis supported these observations as the ANOVA revealed a significant effect of Session (F(9,108) = 69.5, p<0.0001) but the effect of Lesion only approached significance (F(1,12) = 3.5, p=0.0853).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: Lesion and Session did not interact in instrumental conditioning in Experiment 1 (F(9,108) = 1.0, p=0.4215).
source: Importantly, Lesion and Session did not interact (F(9,108) = 1.0, p=0.4215), suggesting a similar rate of instrumental acquisition in both groups.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: During sensory-specific satiety in Experiment 1, rats from the IPSI group consumed more food than rats from the CONTRA group (IPSI: 9.9 ± 3.8 g, CONTRA: 5.5 ± 2.6 g, F(1,12) = 6.5, p=0.0254).
source: During sensory-specific satiety, rats from the IPSI group consumed more food than rats from the CONTRA group (IPSI: 9.9 ± 3.8 g, CONTRA: 5.5 ± 2.6 g, F(1,12) = 6.5, p=0.0254).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the outcome devaluation phase of Experiment 1.

claim: During the choice test in Experiment 1, both groups expressed a marked preference for the lever associated with the still valued outcome (F(1,12) = 37.8, p<0.0001).
source: Nevertheless, during the subsequent choice test, both groups expressed a marked preference for the lever associated with the still valued outcome (F(1,12) = 37.8, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the outcome devaluation phase of Experiment 1.

claim: The preference for the valued outcome in Experiment 1 did not vary as a function of lesion status.
source: This preference did not vary as a function of lesion status as neither the main effect of Lesion (F(1,12) = 1.9, p=0.1957) nor the Lesion X Devaluation interaction (F(1,12) = 0.0, p=0.9530) approached significance.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The post-test consumption assays in Experiment 1 confirmed that devaluation was effective for both groups.
source: The post-test consumption assays shown in Figure 3C confirmed that devaluation was effective for both groups and that rats in the IPSI and CONTRA groups consumed a similar amount for both the valued and the devalued outcomes (Devaluation, F(1,12) = 16.5, p=0.0016; Lesion, Lesion X Devaluation, F < 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the outcome devaluation phase of Experiment 1, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: During reversal training in Experiment 1, all rats maintained a high level of instrumental responding, comparable to that attained at the end of the initial instrumental phase.
source: During that phase, all rats maintained a high level of instrumental responding, comparable to that attained at the end of the initial instrumental phase (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the reversal phase of Experiment 1, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Responding slightly increased during the five reversal sessions in Experiment 1, in a comparable manner across all groups.
source: Responding slightly increased during these five sessions, in a comparable manner across all groups.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the reversal phase of Experiment 1.

claim: There was a significant effect of Session during reversal training in Experiment 1 (F(14, 48)=8.1, p<0.0001).
source: The ANOVA revealed a significant effect of Session (F(14, 48)=8.1, p<0.0001) but not of Lesion (F < 1) or Lesion X Session interaction (F(4,68) = 1.1, p=0.3781).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of the reversal phase in Experiment 1.

claim: During the choice test after reversal in Experiment 1, all rats expressed a marked preference for the action leading to the still valued outcome.
source: During the choice test conducted under extinction conditions (Figure 3E), all rats expressed a marked preference for the action leading to the still valued outcome, showing that they succeeded in updating action-outcome contingencies.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the post-reversal devaluation phase of Experiment 1, with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Rats in Experiment 1 succeeded in updating action-outcome contingencies after reversal.
source: During the choice test conducted under extinction conditions (Figure 3E), all rats expressed a marked preference for the action leading to the still valued outcome, showing that they succeeded in updating action-outcome contingencies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results of the post-reversal devaluation phase in Experiment 1.

claim: There was a main effect of Devaluation in the post-reversal choice test in Experiment 1 (F(1,12) = 11.9, p=0.0048).
source: We found a main effect of Devaluation (F(1,12) = 11.9, p=0.0048) but no effect or Lesion or Lesion X Devaluation interaction (Fs <1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of the post-reversal devaluation phase in Experiment 1.

claim: Disconnecting the OFC from the MD did not alter instrumental conditioning or the ability to update action-outcome contingencies.
source: Collectively, these data show that disconnecting the OFC from the MD did not alter instrumental conditioning or the ability to update action-outcome contingencies.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 1.

claim: Instrumental conditioning gradually developed over the 10 consecutive training sessions for both groups in Experiment 2.
source: As in Experiment 1, instrumental conditioning gradually developed over the 10 consecutive training sessions for both groups (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from Experiment 2, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Instrumental performance appeared similar for both groups in Experiment 2.
source: In this instance, instrumental performance appeared similar for both groups.
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from Experiment 2.

claim: There was a significant effect of Session on instrumental conditioning in Experiment 2 (F(9,153) = 74.1, p<0.0001).
source: The ANOVA conducted on these data support this observation as we found a significant effect of Session (F(9,153) = 74.1, p<0.0001) but not Lesion or Lesion X Session interaction (Fs <1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: During the choice test after initial devaluation in Experiment 2, both groups expressed a marked preference for the lever associated with the still valued outcome (F(1,17) = 29.2, p<0.0001).
source: As observed previously, both groups expressed a marked preference for the lever associated with the still valued outcome (F(1,17) = 29.2, p<0.0001.).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the outcome devaluation phase of Experiment 2.

claim: The preference for the valued outcome in Experiment 2 did not vary as a function of lesion group.
source: Again, this preference did not vary as a function of lesion group as neither the main effect of Lesion nor that of the Lesion X Devaluation interaction were significant (Fs <1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The post-test consumption assays in Experiment 2 confirmed that devaluation was effective for both groups.
source: The post-test consumption assays shown in Figure 4C confirmed that devaluation was effective for both groups and that rats in the IPSI and CONTRA groups consumed similar amounts of both the valued and the devalued outcomes (Devaluation, F(1,17) = 39.5, p<0.0001; Lesion, F(1,17) = 1.8, p=0.1884; Lesion X Devaluation, F(1,17) = 2.2, p=0.1527).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the outcome devaluation phase of Experiment 2, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: During reversal training in Experiment 2, all rats maintained a high level of instrumental responding that did not differ between groups.
source: During that phase, all rats maintained a high level of instrumental responding (Figure 4D) that did not differ between groups (Lesion, F < 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the reversal phase of Experiment 2, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Rats from the CONTRA group in Experiment 2 appeared to respond similarly for both outcomes after reversal while the IPSI group expressed a clear preference for the action earning the still valued outcome.
source: Rats from the CONTRA group appear to respond similarly for both outcomes while the IPSI group expressed a clear preference for the action earning the still valued outcome.
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the post-reversal devaluation phase of Experiment 2.

claim: There was a main effect of Devaluation in the post-reversal choice test in Experiment 2 (F(1,17) = 10.2, p=0.0054).
source: Indeed, we found a main effect of Devaluation (F(1,17) = 10.2, p=0.0054) and a marginal effect of Lesion (F(1,17) = 4.0, p=0.0623) but also, critically, a significant Lesion X Devaluation interaction (F(1,17) = 5.6, p=0.0296).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of the post-reversal devaluation phase in Experiment 2.

claim: There was a significant Lesion X Devaluation interaction in the post-reversal choice test in Experiment 2 (F(1,17) = 5.6, p=0.0296).
source: Indeed, we found a main effect of Devaluation (F(1,17) = 10.2, p=0.0054) and a marginal effect of Lesion (F(1,17) = 4.0, p=0.0623) but also, critically, a significant Lesion X Devaluation interaction (F(1,17) = 5.6, p=0.0296).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of the post-reversal devaluation phase in Experiment 2.

claim: Devaluation reached significance for the IPSI group (F(1,8) = 11.3, p=0.0099) but not the CONTRA group (F < 1) in Experiment 2.
source: Additional analyses confirmed that Devaluation reached significance for the IPSI (F(1,8) = 11.3, p=0.0099) but not the CONTRA group (F < 1) indicating that rats from the CONTRA group were unable to display adaptive responding.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of the post-reversal devaluation phase in Experiment 2.

claim: Rats from the CONTRA group in Experiment 2 were unable to display adaptive responding after reversal.
source: Additional analyses confirmed that Devaluation reached significance for the IPSI (F(1,8) = 11.3, p=0.0099) but not the CONTRA group (F < 1) indicating that rats from the CONTRA group were unable to display adaptive responding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical results of the post-reversal devaluation phase in Experiment 2.

claim: The devaluation procedure was effective for both groups in the post-reversal phase of Experiment 2.
source: Results from the post-test consumption assay confirmed that the devaluation procedure was effective for both groups (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the post-reversal devaluation phase of Experiment 2, with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: Both groups in Experiment 2 consumed significantly more of the valued outcome than the devalued outcome in the post-reversal consumption test.
source: Nevertheless, simple effect contrasts conducted on the interaction confirmed that both groups consumed significantly more of the valued outcome than the devalued outcome (Devaluation, IPSI: F(1.8) = 53, p<0.0001), CONTRA: F(1,9) = 117.3, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of the post-reversal consumption test in Experiment 2.

claim: The behavior displayed by rats from the CONTRA group during the final test after reversal was in clear contrast with that exhibited during the prior choice test.
source: In summary, the behavior displayed by rats from the CONTRA group during the final test after reversal was in clear contrast with that exhibited during the prior choice test, suggesting an inability to update action-outcome contingency.
evidence: This is a summary observation comparing behavioral results across different phases of Experiment 2.

claim: Rats from the CONTRA group in Experiment 2 showed an inability to update action-outcome contingency after reversal.
source: In summary, the behavior displayed by rats from the CONTRA group during the final test after reversal was in clear contrast with that exhibited during the prior choice test, suggesting an inability to update action-outcome contingency.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results of Experiment 2.

claim: Functional interactions between the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) and the medial prefrontal cortex are essential for goal-directed decision-making.
source: In a recent study, we showed that functional interactions between the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) and the medial prefrontal cortex are essential for goal-directed decision-making (Alcaraz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2018).

claim: The MD connects with the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
source: As the MD also connects with the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a region now known to play a role in goal-directed behavior (Parkes et al., 2018), the present study primarily aimed to extend our prior findings by focusing on MD-OFC interactions.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge, also supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The OFC is a region now known to play a role in goal-directed behavior.
source: As the MD also connects with the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a region now known to play a role in goal-directed behavior (Parkes et al., 2018), the present study primarily aimed to extend our prior findings by focusing on MD-OFC interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Parkes et al., 2018).

claim: Disconnecting the OFC from the Sub produced a specific role in guiding choice after action-outcome contingency reversal.
source: The results clearly indicated a specific role for the OFC-Sub circuit in guiding choice after action-outcome contingency reversal.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 2.

claim: The data suggest an important role for the OFC-Sub thalamocortical circuit in goal-directed behavior.
source: Taken as a whole, the data suggest an important role for this thalamocortical circuit in goal-directed behavior and further underscore the functional importance of a still poorly known thalamic region.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The MD is now acknowledged as a major partner of the prefrontal cortex for cognition, from rodent to primate, including humans.
source: The MD is now acknowledged as a major partner of the prefrontal cortex for cognition, from rodent to primate, including humans (Bradfield et al., 2013; Browning et al., 2015; Wolff et al., 2015; Parnaudeau et al., 2018; Pergola et al., 2018; Rikhye et al., 2018b; Wolff and Vann, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Most experimental studies have examined MD's functional interactions with the medial prefrontal cortex, thus neglecting the potential importance of its abundant connections with the OFC.
source: However, to date, most experimental studies have examined its functional interactions with the medial prefrontal cortex (Bolkan et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2017; Alcaraz et al., 2018; Marton et al., 2018; Rikhye et al., 2018a), thus neglecting the potential importance of its abundant connections with the OFC (Alcaraz et al., 2016; Murphy and Deutch, 2018).
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The present study does not support the idea that OFC-MD interactions are important for goal-directed behavior.
source: The present study does not support the idea that these interactions are important for goal-directed behavior, even in a setup known to engage OFC functions (Parkes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 1.

claim: Both MD and OFC neurons were found to code for task-relevant elements in an odor-discrimination task.
source: The functional relevance of the OFC-MD connections has been documented in other settings as both MD and OFC neurons were found to code for task-relevant elements in an odor-discrimination task (Courtiol and Wilson, 2016); however, this feature was not affected by inhibition of the corticothalamic pathway (Courtiol et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Courtiol and Wilson, 2016).

claim: Task-relevant coding in MD and OFC neurons was not affected by inhibition of the corticothalamic pathway.
source: The functional relevance of the OFC-MD connections has been documented in other settings as both MD and OFC neurons were found to code for task-relevant elements in an odor-discrimination task (Courtiol and Wilson, 2016); however, this feature was not affected by inhibition of the corticothalamic pathway (Courtiol et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Courtiol et al., 2019).

claim: In the primate, disconnecting the MD from the ventrolateral and orbital cortex impairs adaptive decision-making after selective outcome devaluation.
source: In the primate, disconnecting the MD from the ventrolateral and orbital cortex impairs adaptive decision-making after selective outcome devaluation (Browning et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Browning et al., 2015).

claim: Disconnecting the MD from the medial prefrontal cortex impairs adaptive decision-making after selective outcome devaluation in rodents.
source: By contrast, we observed the same effect after disconnecting the MD from the medial prefrontal cortex (Alcaraz et al., 2018) but not the OFC (present data).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2018).

claim: The functional parcellation of the OFC is now becoming clearer.
source: This certainly calls for further work to document the functional equivalence of prefrontal territories in rodent and primate (Laubach et al., 2018), especially when the functional parcellation of the OFC is now becoming clearer (Izquierdo, 2017; Panayi and Killcross, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent literature (Izquierdo, 2017; Panayi and Killcross, 2018).

claim: OFC-MD connections may support situations where choice is guided by stimulus-outcome associations.
source: Thus, more work is needed to identify the functions that may be supported by connections between the OFC and the MD. An attractive prospect could be to rely on situations where choice is guided by stimulus-outcome associations, as previously suggested (Ostlund and Balleine, 2008; Wolff et al., 2015; Alcaraz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Disconnecting the OFC from the Sub did not impair the ability to learn action-outcome associations and to use this information to guide choice.
source: Disconnecting the OFC from the Sub did not impair the ability to learn action-outcome associations and to use this information to guide choice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 2.

claim: When action-outcome associations were reversed, rats with contralateral lesions of the OFC-Sub pathway were unable to integrate this new information to guide subsequent choice between the two actions.
source: However, when action-outcome associations were reversed, rats with contralateral lesions of the OFC-Sub pathway were unable to integrate this new information to guide subsequent choice between the two actions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 2.

claim: Rats with OFC-Sub disconnection could not accurately segregate multiple action-outcome contingencies.
source: This does not necessarily imply that these animals were unable to notice these changes during the reversal phase. If that was the case they would show a devaluation effect consistent with the original contingencies, which was not observed during that test. Instead, reduced responding was observed for both actions, suggesting that these rats could not accurately segregate multiple action-outcome contingencies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results of Experiment 2.

claim: OFC-Sub disconnection points to a specific deficit in updating contingency information rather than an overall deficit in learning the relationship between actions and their outcomes.
source: Both hypotheses therefore point to a specific deficit in updating contingency information rather than an overall deficit in learning the relationship between actions and their outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results of Experiment 2.

claim: A prior study indicated a deficit in the ability to update stimulus-outcome contingencies in Sub lesioned rats.
source: This is consistent with a prior study indicating a deficit in the ability to update stimulus-outcome contingencies in Sub lesioned rats (Alcaraz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2015).

claim: Connections between the OFC and the Sub are critical to distinguish between learning experiences or task states.
source: Overall, this suggests that connections between the OFC and the Sub are critical to distinguish between learning experiences or task states (Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings, with a citation to related work (Wilson et al., 2014).

claim: The cognitive thalamus critically assists the cortex to ensure that mental representations or cognitive maps are still relevant.
source: It is also consistent with the emerging view that the cognitive thalamus critically assists the cortex to ensure that mental representations or cognitive maps are still relevant (Wolff and Vann, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent literature (Wolff and Vann, 2019).

claim: It is not possible with the lesion disconnection approach to assign specific functions to OFC-to-Sub and Sub-to-OFC pathways.
source: While targeting projection-defined cortical and thalamic neurons previously enabled us to differentiate the functional contribution of thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways (Bolkan et al., 2017; Alcaraz et al., 2018), it is not possible with this lesion approach to assign specific functions to OFC-to-Sub and Sub-to-OFC pathways.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental approach acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Thalamocortical projections are known to be almost exclusively ipsilateral.
source: Moreover, while thalamocortical projections are known to be almost exclusively ipsilateral, returning corticothalamic pathways cross to the other hemisphere (Négyessy et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge, supported by a citation (Négyessy et al., 1998).

claim: Returning corticothalamic pathways cross to the other hemisphere.
source: Moreover, while thalamocortical projections are known to be almost exclusively ipsilateral, returning corticothalamic pathways cross to the other hemisphere (Négyessy et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge, supported by a citation (Négyessy et al., 1998).

claim: Corticothalamic pathways would not be compromised with the lesion disconnection approach.
source: Thus, the latter would not be compromised with the present approach.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: After initial instrumental training, functional interactions between the mPFC and the MD but not the OFC and the Sub are necessary to guide choice based on current goal value.
source: First, distinct thalamocortical circuits appear to support instrumental performance, depending on whether updating of the associative structure of the task is required: after initial instrumental training, functional interactions between the mPFC and the MD but not the OFC and the Sub are necessary to guide choice based on current goal value but the exact opposite pattern is found after action-outcome reversal.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the current study and prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2018).

claim: After action-outcome reversal, functional interactions between the OFC and the Sub but not the mPFC and the MD are necessary to guide choice.
source: First, distinct thalamocortical circuits appear to support instrumental performance, depending on whether updating of the associative structure of the task is required: after initial instrumental training, functional interactions between the mPFC and the MD but not the OFC and the Sub are necessary to guide choice based on current goal value but the exact opposite pattern is found after action-outcome reversal.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the current study and prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2018).

claim: There is a striking double dissociation regarding the functional involvement of the mPFC-MD and the OFC-Sub circuits in instrumental performance.
source: In other words, there is striking double dissociation regarding the functional involvement of the mPFC-MD and the OFC-Sub circuits in instrumental performance.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the current study and prior work.

claim: The results fit well with novel conceptions of the functioning of thalamocortical circuits, emphasizing parallel and synergetic information processing to achieve cognitively relevant functions.
source: This major result fits well with novel conceptions of the functioning of thalamocortical circuits, emphasizing parallel and synergetic information processing to achieve cognitively relevant functions (Rikhye et al., 2018b; Wolff and Vann, 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of recent theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: The Sub appears to be important to update not only stimulus-outcome but also action-outcome associations.
source: Second, the present data are in agreement with a broader conception of OFC functions but they also highlight the contribution of a poorly understood thalamic region. The Sub indeed appears to be important to update not only stimulus-outcome but also action-outcome associations, consistent with the idea that thalamic nuclei may help to shape mental representations (Wolff and Vann, 2019).
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the current study and prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2015), with reference to a theoretical framework (Wolff and Vann, 2019).

claim: Thalamic nuclei may help to shape mental representations.
source: The Sub indeed appears to be important to update not only stimulus-outcome but also action-outcome associations, consistent with the idea that thalamic nuclei may help to shape mental representations (Wolff and Vann, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent literature (Wolff and Vann, 2019).

claim: Thalamic afferents from both the Sub and the MD terminate within the same OFC loci.
source: As thalamic afferents from both the Sub and the MD terminate within the same OFC loci (Alcaraz et al., 2015; Alcaraz et al., 2016), this would provide an ideal venue to investigate the functional relevance of convergence in cognition (Man et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Alcaraz et al., 2015; Alcaraz et al., 2016).

claim: Rather than acting as isolated loops assigned to specific functions, thalamocortical circuits would be better described as supporting each other in the face of changing circumstances.
source: In conclusion, the present study complements prior findings to broaden our understanding of the functioning of thalamocortical circuits. Rather than acting as isolated loops assigned to specific functions, they would be better described as supporting each other in the face of changing circumstances.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and their integration with prior work.

claim: Cortical areas may communicate directly but also indirectly through the thalamus.
source: An influential view posits that cortical areas may communicate directly but also indirectly through the thalamus (Sherman, 2016; Sherman, 2018; Usrey and Sherman, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent theoretical work (Sherman, 2016; Sherman, 2018; Usrey and Sherman, 2019).

claim: Convergent and divergent thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways may help to recruit the currently relevant circuit and/or to gate the most meaningful inputs.
source: One consequence of this functional organization is that convergent and divergent thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways may help to recruit the currently relevant circuit and/or to gate the most meaningful inputs (Wolff and Vann, 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical frameworks, supported by a citation (Wolff and Vann, 2019).

claim: Ensuring the accuracy of mental representations over time, and over changing circumstances, likely necessitates the cooperation of multiple circuits.
source: Thus, ensuring the accuracy of mental representations over time, and over changing circumstances, likely necessitates the cooperation of multiple circuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and theoretical considerations.

claim: The findings suggest cautious use of causality concepts to interpret data in contemporary neurosciences.
source: As noted previously, this suggests cautious use of causality concepts to interpret data in contemporary neurosciences (Yoshihara and Yoshihara, 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological/philosophical point supported by a citation (Yoshihara and Yoshihara, 2018).

claim: Thalamic research has now entered a new era.
source: Thalamic research has now entered a new era and we can expect in the coming years a more systematic assessment of thalamocortical circuits that should provide important insights to better apprehend mental conditions best described as connectivity disorders such as schizophrenia (Anticevic et al., 2014), obsessive-compulsive behaviors (Greenberg et al., 2010; Monteiro and Feng, 2016) or addiction (Balleine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Schizophrenia is best described as a connectivity disorder.
source: Thalamic research has now entered a new era and we can expect in the coming years a more systematic assessment of thalamocortical circuits that should provide important insights to better apprehend mental conditions best described as connectivity disorders such as schizophrenia (Anticevic et al., 2014), obsessive-compulsive behaviors (Greenberg et al., 2010; Monteiro and Feng, 2016) or addiction (Balleine et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Anticevic et al., 2014).

source: Thalamic research has now entered a new era and we can expect in the coming years a more systematic assessment of thalamocortical circuits that should provide important insights to better apprehend mental conditions best described as connectivity disorders such as schizophrenia (Anticevic et al., 2014), obsessive-compulsive behaviors (Greenberg et al., 2010; Monteiro and Feng, 2016) or addiction (Balleine et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Greenberg et al., 2010; Monteiro and Feng, 2016).

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Balleine et al., 2015).

claim: 48 male Long Evans rats weighing 275 g to 300 g at surgery were used in the study.
source: 48 male Long Evans rats weighing 275 g to 300 g at surgery were obtained from Centre d'Elevage Janvier (France).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the subjects used in the study.

claim: Rats were initially housed in pairs.
source: Rats were initially housed in pairs and accustomed to the laboratory facility for two weeks before the beginning of the experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about animal housing.

claim: The experimental protocols received approval #5012053-A from the local Ethics Committee on December 7, 2012.
source: The experimental protocols received approval #5012053-A from the local Ethics Committee on December 7, 2012.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: After histological verification, the final group sizes were: IPSI n = 7, CONTRA n = 7 for the OFC-MD disconnection.
source: After histological verification (see below), the final group sizes were: IPSI n = 7, CONTRA n = 7 for the OFC-MD disconnection and IPSI n = 9, CONTRA n = 10 for the OFC-Sub disconnection.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the final sample sizes.

claim: After histological verification, the final group sizes were: IPSI n = 9, CONTRA n = 10 for the OFC-Sub disconnection.
source: After histological verification (see below), the final group sizes were: IPSI n = 7, CONTRA n = 7 for the OFC-MD disconnection and IPSI n = 9, CONTRA n = 10 for the OFC-Sub disconnection.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the final sample sizes.

claim: Rats were anaesthetized with 4% Isoflurane for surgery.
source: Rats were anaesthetized with 4% Isoflurane and placed in a stereotaxic frame with atraumatic ear bars (Kopf, Tujunga, CA) in a flatskull position.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the surgical procedure.

claim: Anaesthesia was maintained with 1.5–2% Isoflurane during surgery.
source: Anaesthesia was maintained with 1.5–2% Isoflurane and complemented by subcutaneous administration of buprenorphin (Buprecare, 0.05 mg/kg).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the surgical procedure.

claim: Unilateral neurotoxic lesions were performed using multiple NMDA micro-injections to disconnect the OFC from its thalamic afferents.
source: To disconnect the OFC from its two main thalamic afferents, unilateral neurotoxic lesions were performed in contralateral hemispheres using multiple NMDA micro-injections.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the lesion procedure.

claim: 20 µg/µl NMDA in artificial cerebrospinal fluid was used for lesions.
source: 20 µg/µl NMDA (Sigma-Aldrich) in artificial cerebrospinal fluid (CMA Microdialysis AB, Solna, Sweden) was pressure injected (Picospritzer, General Valve Corporation, Fairfield, NJ) into the brain through a glass micropipette (outside diameter approximately 100 µm) and polyethylene tubing.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the lesion procedure.

claim: Rats were given at least 10 days of recovery before behavioral testing.
source: Rats were given at least 10 days of recovery before behavioral testing.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental timeline.

claim: The behavioral design is adapted from Parkes et al. (2018).
source: The design is adapted from Parkes et al. (2018) and consists in providing a choice test following outcome devaluation after an initial instrumental training phase (green), but also after reversal of action-outcome contingencies (orange).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral paradigm, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Rats were first habituated to the magazine dispenser through two daily sessions of magazine training for 2 days.
source: Rats were first habituated to the magazine dispenser through two daily sessions of magazine training for 2 days.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral procedure.

claim: Instrumental conditioning consisted of ten daily sessions.
source: After magazine training, instrumental conditioning began for a total of ten daily sessions, during which rats had to learn the specific, causal association between two responses (left or right lever presses) and the two different outcomes (grain or sucrose pellets).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral procedure.

claim: For the two first instrumental sessions, each action was reinforced on a FR1 schedule.
source: For the two first sessions, each action was reinforced (FR1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral procedure.

claim: Sessions 5 to 7 were performed with a RR10 schedule.
source: Sessions 5 to 7 were performed with a RR10 schedule (probability of receiving an outcome given a response = 0.1) and sessions 8 to 10 with a RR20 (probability of receiving an outcome given a response = 0.05).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral procedure.

claim: Sessions 8 to 10 were performed with a RR20 schedule.
source: Sessions 5 to 7 were performed with a RR10 schedule (probability of receiving an outcome given a response = 0.1) and sessions 8 to 10 with a RR20 (probability of receiving an outcome given a response = 0.05).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral procedure.

claim: Rats were placed in a plastic feeding cage containing free access to 15 g of one of the two outcomes for one hour of specific satiety-induced devaluation.
source: The day after the last session of instrumental training, rats were placed in a plastic feeding cage containing free access to 15 g of one of the two outcomes for one hour of specific satiety-induced devaluation.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the devaluation procedure.

claim: The extinction test lasted 10 minutes.
source: Immediately after, rats were put in the operant cages for a 10 min extinction test.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral procedure.

claim: During the extinction test, both actions were available but were unrewarded.
source: During the test, both actions were available but were unrewarded.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the behavioral procedure.

claim: The extinction test ensured that rats were using representations of the action-outcome contingencies and outcome value to guide their behavior.
source: This ensured that rats were using representations of the action-outcome contingencies and outcome value to guide their behavior.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the extinction test procedure.

claim: After the extinction test, rats had free access to 10 g of each outcome for 10 min in the consumption test.
source: After the extinction test, rats were returned to the plastic feeding cages. They had free access to 10 g of each outcome for 10 min.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the consumption test procedure.

claim: Rats received five reversal sessions in total on an RR20 schedule of reinforcement.
source: Rats received five reversal sessions in total on an RR20 schedule of reinforcement.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the reversal training procedure.

claim: Histological analysis of the lesions was performed under the microscope by two experimenters blind to lesion conditions.
source: Histological analysis of the lesions was performed under the microscope by two experimenters (VF and MW) blind to lesion conditions.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the histological analysis.

claim: The data were submitted to ANOVAs on StatView software.
source: The data were submitted to ANOVAs on StatView software (SAS Institute Inc).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the statistical analysis.

claim: The alpha value for rejection of the null hypothesis was 0.05.
source: The alpha value for rejection of the null hypothesis was 0.05.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the statistical analysis.
